chunks: Interrupt inside an ISR: nesting. The question: What happens if an ISR gets called while in an ISR? How can this be avoided?
Nesting means one interrupt handler gets interrupted by a more urgent one. The urgent handler runs inside the first, then control goes back to the first.
On ARM Cortex-M chips, the interrupt controller compares priorities: a higher priority preempts, and an equal or lower one waits.
Nesting serves urgent events quickly, but it costs memory and creates new hazards.
A doctor is treating a patient when an emergency call comes in. She pauses, handles the emergency, and returns to the patient. A less urgent call waits until she is free.
Each paused patient needs a note saying where she stopped, so the more she is interrupted, the taller the pile of notes.
One difference: the same patient calling again does not interrupt her. It is noted once for later.
On Cortex-M the NVIC walks exactly this decision. A masked or lower-priority source never interrupts the running handler; it queues.
Only a strictly higher-priority, unmasked source nests.
Priority: a number saying how urgent an interrupt is. On Cortex-M a lower number is more urgent. Preempt: to interrupt a running handler so a more urgent one runs first.
Pending: recorded by the hardware and waiting for its turn. Stack: memory where the CPU saves what it was doing. Each nested level uses some.
Handler A (priority 3) is running. Event B (priority 1) arrives. Since 1 is more urgent than 3, the hardware saves A's state (at least 32 bytes of stack) and runs B.
When B finishes, A resumes. Now event C (priority 3) arrives during A. It has the same priority, so it waits as pending until A returns.
On an AVR chip the hardware blocks all interrupts on entry, so nothing nests unless the code turns them back on. That is the whole idea.
"On a Cortex-M it depends on priority. A higher-priority interrupt preempts: the hardware stacks another frame, runs it, and returns into the first ISR, which is nesting.
Equal or lower priority waits as pending and runs after, and the same interrupt can't preempt itself, so a repeat just pends.
On AVR the global interrupt flag is cleared on entry, so no nesting unless you re-enable.
To avoid problems, set priorities deliberately, keep ISRs short, protect shared data, and budget stack."
